subject: Compiler Design
topic: Compiler Architecture, Lexical Analysis, and Tokenization
stem: How many tokens are generated by a lexical analyzer for the C statement: `printf("Sum = %d\n", x + 10);`?
explanation: The lexical analyzer decomposes the statement into 8 tokens: (1) `printf` [identifier], (2) `(` [left parenthesis], (3) `"Sum = %d\n"` [string literal as a single token], (4) `,` [comma], (5) `x` [identifier], (6) `+` [addition operator], (7) `10` [integer constant], and (8) `);` [right parenthesis and semicolon count as two tokens: `)` and `;`]. Total = 8 tokens.
reviewNote: Verified tokenization rules for identifiers, literals, and punctuation symbols.

stem: Which compiler phase is primarily responsible for stripping comments, removing whitespace, and maintaining line numbers for error diagnostic reporting?
explanation: Lexical Analysis (the scanner) reads the source character stream, strips out unnecessary comments and white spaces, tracks line numbers for error messaging, and passes a clean stream of tokens to the syntax analyzer.

stem: Consider the grammar with start symbol S: S -> A B, A -> a A | ε, B -> b. What is the FOLLOW(A) set?
explanation: In production S -> A B, non-terminal B immediately follows A. Therefore, FOLLOW(A) = FIRST(B) = { b }. Since FIRST(B) does not contain ε, no further symbols are added. Note that FOLLOW sets never contain ε.
reviewNote: Verified FOLLOW set calculation for nullable grammars.

subject: Compiler Design
topic: Context-Free Grammars, LL(1) Parsing, and FIRST & FOLLOW Sets
stem: Which of the following grammar properties automatically PREVENTS a Context-Free Grammar from being LL(1)?

options.text: Having terminal symbols on the right-hand side

explanation: Left recursion (immediate or indirect) causes top-down predictive parsers to enter an infinite loop when expanding production rules. Hence, any left-recursive grammar is strictly non-LL(1).
reviewNote: Verified LL(1) necessary condition regarding left recursion.

attribution: GATE CS LALR State Merging Analysis
subject: Compiler Design
topic: Bottom-Up Parsing and LR Parsers: LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1), and CLR(1)
stem: When canonical LR(1) states with identical LR(0) cores are merged to construct an LALR(1) parser table, which of the following conflict behaviors can occur?

options.text: Shift/Reduce conflicts can be introduced, but Reduce/Reduce conflicts cannot.
Reduce/Reduce conflicts can be introduced, but Shift/Reduce conflicts CANNOT.
Both Shift/Reduce and Reduce/Reduce conflicts can be introduced.
Neither Shift/Reduce nor Reduce/Reduce conflicts can ever be introduced.

explanation: Merging states with identical core LR(0) items preserves shift actions completely, ensuring that NO new Shift/Reduce conflicts can ever be introduced. However, combining lookahead sets for completed items can cause lookaheads to overlap, which may introduce Reduce/Reduce conflicts.
reviewNote: Verified LALR state merging conflict creation properties.

attribution: Standard LR Parser Expressive Power Hierarchy
subject: Compiler Design
topic: Bottom-Up Parsing and LR Parsers: LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1), and CLR(1)
stem: What is the correct expressive power containment hierarchy among bottom-up LR parser families?
explanation: LR(0) is the least powerful parser family (no lookahead). SLR(1) adds FOLLOW set lookaheads. LALR(1) uses item-specific lookaheads with state merging. Canonical LR(1) (CLR(1)) is the most expressive parser family without state merging.

attribution: GATE CS Syntax-Directed Translation Attribute Rules
subject: Compiler Design
stem: In an L-attributed Syntax-Directed Definition (SDD), an inherited attribute for symbol X_j in production A -> X_1 X_2 ... X_n can depend on which attributes?

options.text: Only attributes of children nodes below X_j
Attributes of parent head A and sibling symbols to the LEFT of X_j (X_1 ... X_{j-1})
Attributes of sibling symbols to the RIGHT of X_j (X_{j+1} ... X_n)
Any attribute of any node across the entire parse tree

explanation: L-attributed definitions enforce a left-to-right evaluation order. An inherited attribute for X_j can depend only on parent attributes of A or left siblings X_1, ..., X_{j-1}. Dependency on right siblings is strictly forbidden.

subject: Compiler Design
stem: Which class of Syntax-Directed Definitions contains ONLY synthesized attributes and can be evaluated during bottom-up parsing using a parser stack?
explanation: S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes. Because synthesized attributes are computed strictly from child node attributes, they can be evaluated naturally during bottom-up LR reductions by storing attribute values on the parser stack.

subject: Compiler Design
topic: Intermediate Code Generation (ICG): Three-Address Code, Quadruples, and Triples
stem: Why are Quadruples generally preferred over Triples in optimizing compiler backends?

options.text: Quadruples require less memory than Triples.
Quadruples use explicit result names, allowing instructions to be reordered safely during optimization.
Triples cannot represent conditional jump instructions.
Quadruples eliminate the need for symbol table lookup.

explanation: Triples reference temporary values implicitly via statement array indices (e.g. `(i)`). Moving or deleting statements during code optimization invalidates these positional pointers. Quadruples use explicit destination variable names, making instruction reordering straightforward.

subject: Compiler Design
topic: Intermediate Code Generation (ICG): Three-Address Code, Quadruples, and Triples
stem: In Three-Address Code (TAC), what is the maximum number of memory operands allowed on the right-hand side of a standard arithmetic assignment statement?
explanation: Three-Address Code instructions have at most three addresses total: one for the destination result on the LHS, and at most two source operands on the RHS (e.g. `x = y op z`).

stem: Which pointer field in an activation record (stack frame) points directly to the activation record of the function that called it?
explanation: The Control Link (or Dynamic Link) points to the stack frame of the caller routine. In contrast, the Access Link (or Static Link) points to the stack frame of the lexically enclosing static scope to resolve non-local variable references.

subject: Compiler Design
topic: Runtime Environments, Memory Layout, and Activation Records
stem: Why does standard dynamic activation record stack memory allocation fail for languages that support first-class nested functions that can be returned?

options.text: Stack frames of returning functions are popped upon return, destroying local variables needed by the returned closure function.
Stack frames cannot hold function pointers.
Control links cannot be stored on a stack.

explanation: If a nested function outlives its parent caller (a closure), the parent's stack frame would be destroyed upon return under LIFO stack allocation. Hence, such languages require heap-allocated activation records.

stem: Consider the Three-Address Code: (1) i = 1, (2) j = 1, (3) t1 = 10 * i, (4) if t1 > 100 goto (7), (5) i = i + 1, (6) goto (3), (7) return. How many basic blocks are formed?
explanation:
Leader identification algorithm:
1. Line 1 is a leader (first statement).
2. Line 3 is a leader (target of jump at line 6).
3. Line 5 is a leader (statement following conditional jump at line 4).
4. Line 7 is a leader (target of jump at line 4).
Leaders are lines 1, 3, 5, 7. The basic blocks are: B1 (lines 1-2), B2 (lines 3-4), B3 (lines 5-6), B4 (line 7). Total = 4 basic blocks.

stem: Replacing an expensive multiplication operation `i * 4` inside an inner loop with a cheap addition operation `t = t + 4` across loop iterations is an example of which code transformation?
explanation: Strength Reduction replaces a computationally expensive operation (multiplication) with an equivalent cheaper operation (addition) across induction variables in loop iterations.

attribution: GATE CS Data-Flow Direction and Meet Operators
subject: Compiler Design
topic: Data-Flow Analysis: Constant Propagation, Liveness Analysis, and CSE
stem: Which of the following correctly characterizes Liveness Analysis in global data-flow analysis?

options.text: Forward data-flow analysis with Intersection meet operator (Must analysis)
Forward data-flow analysis with Union meet operator (May analysis)
Backward data-flow analysis with Union meet operator (May analysis)
Backward data-flow analysis with Intersection meet operator (Must analysis)

explanation: Liveness Analysis propagates information BACKWARD from program exit toward entry points, using Union (∪) as the confluence/meet operator because a variable is live if it is read along AT LEAST ONE future execution path (May analysis).
reviewNote: Verified Liveness Analysis direction and meet operator.

subject: Compiler Design
topic: Data-Flow Analysis: Constant Propagation, Liveness Analysis, and CSE
stem: An expression `x + y` is considered Available at a program point p if which of the following holds?

options.text: `x + y` was evaluated on at least one path leading to p.
`x + y` was evaluated on ALL paths leading to p, and neither x nor y was modified since that evaluation.
`x + y` will be evaluated on all paths after point p.

explanation: Available Expressions is a Forward Must Analysis. An expression `x + y` is available at point p if every execution path reaching p evaluates `x + y`, and no subsequent assignment to `x` or `y` occurs prior to reaching p. This property enables Common Subexpression Elimination.
reviewNote: Verified Available Expressions forward must property.
